title: O Absalom, my son (2 Samuel 19:1)
hookLine: the king weeps for the son who rebelled: "would I had died for thee"
carry: would I had died for thee
tomorrow: The wise woman of Abel (2 Samuel 20:14–22)
last: ONE CHOICE, ON ONE ROAD, TO KEEP WALKING.

lines: DEAL GENTLY WITH THE YOUNG MAN.
cards: Before the battle, the king stands at the gate as his army marches out, and gives one order, loud enough for every soldier to hear: deal gently, for my sake, with the young man, with Absalom.
The fighting is in the forest of Ephraim, and the forest, the text says, devours more people than the sword. A watchman on the wall sees a runner. Then another.
David has one question for each of them, and it isn't about the battle. Is the young man Absalom safe?

teach.b: He wasn't. Riding a mule under a great oak, Absalom caught his head fast in the tree, and the mule went on, leaving him hanging between heaven and earth.
A soldier saw him and wouldn't touch him, because of the king's order. Joab didn't hesitate.
Absalom died there, and they threw him into a pit in the forest and heaped stones over him.
The second runner, a Cushite, answers the king in the gentlest words he can find: may all the king's enemies be as that young man is. David understands.

teach.h: WOULD I HAD DIED FOR THEE.
teach.b: He is shaken, and goes up to the room over the gate and weeps, and as he goes he says: O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! "would I had died for thee", O Absalom, my son, my son!
Over Saul and Jonathan, David made a song. Here there is no song, only broken words circling back to one: my son.
This is the son who stole the people's hearts, drove his father barefoot out of the city, and came after his life.
David's grief has no conditions. He doesn't say, if only he hadn't rebelled. He wishes he had died in his place.
It doesn't stay private. The victory turns to mourning, and soldiers slip back into the city like people ashamed after a defeat. Joab tells the king bluntly he is shaming the men who saved his life.

teach.h: THE KING SITS IN THE GATE.
teach.b: And David gets up and sits in the gate. A father's grief that holds nothing back, and a king who still has to face his people.

how: Jews read David's lament for Absalom as part of the book of Samuel; in Jewish Bibles the cry is the opening verse of chapter 19, while English Bibles that follow the King James numbering place it at the end of chapter 18.

o: David's cry of grief for the son who rebelled
a curse David spoke over his rebel son
a call to his son to surrender at last

p: deal gently with the young man
where David went up to weep

s: David asked the runners first about the battle
his question to each was: is the young man Absalom safe?
the text says Absalom's head caught in the oak
his head caught fast, and the mule went on without him.
he cried my son, my son, and wished he had died in Absalom's place.

games.q: you're the runner. Absalom is dead, and the king asks you: is the young man safe? what do you say?
o: may all the king's enemies be as that young man is.
the battle is won; ask someone else.
games.why: the Cushite answers gently, without saying the word dead. David understands, and goes up to weep.

practice: Bring to mind a loss you've told yourself you shouldn't feel so much, like someone who walked away.

If your grief keeps adding a but, they chose it, but, I should be over it, but, drop the but for a few breaths and let yourself miss what you miss. If you pray, you can remember them before God by name.

wordCard.voice: O Absalom. A father's cry over the son who rebelled against him, my son, my son, wishing he had died instead. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: my son Absalom, from David's cry in 2 Samuel 19:1.
